note: The gate itself is speaking. Like many ancient and medieval inscriptions, it talks in the first person. The canto opens on its words with no introduction, so the reader meets them as Dante does.
Hell is pictured as a city, with gates, walls and citizens: the dark opposite of the City of God, as Christian writers called Heaven.
Hell, for Dante, is not cruelty but justice: each soul gets what it chose. The gate goes on to claim that love made it too, the hardest idea in the poem for many modern readers.
Power, wisdom and love are the Trinity: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. All three persons of God made Hell.
The angels, the heavens and the first matter, which God made directly and which last forever. Hell was made next, for the rebel angels when they fell, before any human being existed.

quote: Abandon all hope, you who enter here!
note: Perhaps the most quoted line in the poem. In Italian: Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate. Loss of hope is what defines the damned. The souls in Purgatory suffer too, but they know their pain will end.
It has no door and no guard. Virgil says in Inferno 8 that it has stood open since Christ broke it down when he descended into Hell. Anyone can walk in.
Dante's Italian says the meaning is "hard" for him: hard to understand, or harsh and frightening. He is alive, and the words seem meant for him as well.
A phrase from Aristotle: the good the mind is made for is truth. For Dante the highest truth is God, and the damned have lost sight of him forever.
Hell is underground and has no sky. Dante won't see the stars again until the last line of Inferno. Each of the poem's three parts ends on the word "stars".

The neutrals, who never took a side for good or evil. Their place is Dante's own invention: an entrance hall inside the gate but before the river, not properly part of Hell. Revelation speaks the same way of the lukewarm, whom God spits out of his mouth (3:16).
Angels who took neither side when Lucifer rebelled against God. They are not in the Bible. Dante draws on a popular legend of neutral angels.

quote: even the damned would gain glory over them
note: The real sinners at least did something. Beside these souls they could feel proud of themselves, and Hell won't give them that satisfaction.
A proverbial line in Italy: Non ragioniam di lor, ma guarda e passa. Dante obeys. He names no one in this crowd, so that they stay as forgotten as they made themselves.
The first example of contrapasso, the rule that each punishment mirrors its sin. Those who would follow no cause in life now run forever behind a flag that stands for nothing and never stops.
The cowards far outnumber the great sinners. T. S. Eliot borrowed the line in The Waste Land for the crowd of office workers crossing London Bridge.

quote: Who made the great refusal through cowardice
context: Dante gives no name. Most commentators since his own century have taken this to be Pope Celestine V, whose abdication opened the way for Boniface VIII, the pope Dante blamed for his exile. Others have proposed Pontius Pilate, who washed his hands of Christ's fate, or Esau.

note: To live, for Dante, is to choose. Those who never chose never really lived.
Nothing ever stung these souls into action in life. Now insects goad them on without rest, and the only things they produce, blood and tears, feed the worms.
A forecast of what lies ahead. The deepest part of Dante's Hell is not fire but a frozen lake.

quote: A lighter boat must carry you
note: Charon sees that Dante isn't damned, and unwittingly foretells his salvation. Saved souls are carried to Purgatory by an angel, in a boat so light it barely touches the water (Purgatorio 2).

context: Dante takes him almost whole from Book 6 of the Aeneid, where he also tries to turn away a living passenger. Virgil made him a filthy old god. Dante makes him a demon.

quote: This is willed where there is power
note: It is willed in Heaven, where whatever is willed can be done. God and Heaven are not named in Hell. Virgil uses the same formula as a kind of passport, and repeats it to Minos in Canto 5.
The Acheron, wide and slow here. Livid is the dark gray-blue of lead or of a bruise.

quote: They cursed God and their parents
note: The damned blame everyone and everything except themselves. No one in Dante's Hell repents.

Borrowed from the Aeneid, where the dead crowding the riverbank are as many as the leaves that fall at the first frost. Dante makes the leaves drop one by one, as the souls do, each going down separately.

context: Adam's "seed" is the human race. The evil seed are those of his descendants who die damned.

quote: like a bird to its call
note: An image from falconry and bird-catching: a trained bird comes down to its master's signal.
The damned hurry toward their punishment. They chose their sin in life, and God's justice now makes them want what they chose. Hell is the soul getting its own way.
Charon's anger was good news. Only the damned cross here, so if he refuses Dante, Dante is not one of them.
An earthquake, with wind and a flash of red light. Medieval science, following Aristotle, held that earthquakes came from winds trapped inside the earth.

quote: I fell like someone seized by sleep
note: Dante faints, and wakes in Canto 4 on the far bank. How he crossed the Acheron is never told. It is the first of several swoons and sleeps that carry him over a threshold.
